title: IBM CEO Says Delayed Enterprise Software Deals Are Returning as AI Spending Panic Eases
excerpt: Arvind Krishna told investors that one-third of deals deferred during a rocky second quarter have already closed, calling the slowdown a temporary shift rather than a permanent loss of demand.
body:
• IBM CEO Arvind Krishna said one-third of large enterprise software deals that slipped in Q2 2026 have already closed in Q3, framing the slowdown as a deferral rather than demand destruction.
  • Customers redirected budgets toward servers, storage, and memory to lock in AI-related hardware before prices rose by nearly 60%, squeezing IBM's software and mainframe sales.
  • IBM cut its full-year revenue growth forecast from over 5% to a 4%-5% range, and mainframe infrastructure revenue fell 42% in the quarter.
  • The company's stock has dropped roughly 30% since the pre-announcement on July 14, when Krishna acknowledged IBM had "faltered" in adapting to the spending shift.

What Happened

IBM chief executive Arvind Krishna moved to calm rattled investors on Thursday, insisting that the enterprise software deals delayed during the company's troubled second quarter are already flowing back. Speaking on Fox Business, Krishna disclosed that one-third of the large contracts that fell out of Q2 have been signed in the current quarter.

https://x.com/FoxBusiness/status/2080376130347909479

"One-third of all the deals that fell out of the second quarter have already come back. So that gives us a signal, maybe not proof yet, but a signal that that was indeed just a deferral for a few weeks, not a destruction."

— Arvind Krishna, CEO, IBM

The reassurance comes after IBM suffered its steepest single-day stock decline in over a century on July 14, when Krishna told investors in a letter that the company had "faltered" and that "numerous large deals" had slipped. Shares dropped 25% that day and have continued to slide since.

Why Customers Pulled Back

The root cause, according to Krishna, was a sharp spike in semiconductor and AI infrastructure prices. Hardware costs surged roughly 60% year over year, prompting Fortune 100 clients to redirect their quarterly capital expenditure toward servers, storage, and memory to secure supply-constrained equipment before prices climbed further.

"When those are going up at 60% year over year, people are worried, and that's the classic inflation — if it's going to go up that much, I need to buy that now," Krishna explained. "And so I redirect my capex to that side."

That reallocation left less money for software licenses and mainframe refreshes. IBM's Q2 results, reported on Wednesday, confirmed the damage: software revenue growth slowed to 5%, consulting revenue was flat, and infrastructure revenue fell 7%. Mainframe sales specifically dropped 42%, according to the Wall Street Journal. The company missed both revenue and profit expectations for the quarter.

Revised Outlook and Market Reaction

IBM cut its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast from over 5% to a range of 4% to 5%. The midpoint falls below the analyst consensus estimate of 4.8% growth, which would translate to roughly $70.77 billion in revenue, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.

CFRA analyst Brooks Idlet offered a more measured assessment: "For the broader software sector, this should be treated as a positive print, with IBM's software woes more likely to reflect specific IBM-related hardware issues, as management outlined in its investor letter last week."

IBM's predicament highlights a widening divide in the tech sector. Pure-play AI beneficiaries such as Nvidia continue to post strong results, while companies with heavy exposure to traditional enterprise IT — including Salesforce, Workday, and Snowflake — face buyer hesitation. IBM sits squarely in the latter camp, even as it touts its own AI progress through Watsonx and hybrid cloud services.

The Broader AI Spending Squeeze

The dynamics squeezing IBM mirror a pattern the industry saw during the cloud migration wave. Companies cannot spend the same dollar twice. When data-center capital expenditure surges to secure GPUs and AI infrastructure, other line items — including software renewals and mainframe upgrades — shrink.

Krishna acknowledged that IBM does not expect supply-chain constraints in the AI infrastructure market to ease anytime soon. "Everyone in the industry is saying this will extend for a period of time," IBM CFO James Kavanaugh said on the earnings call.

The company is now shifting its sales strategy to prevent a repeat. Krishna said he is "confident that most of those deals will close within six months" and emphasized that artificial intelligence remains a major growth driver for IBM's own business, with AI-related consulting engagements forming a bright spot.

What It Means for the Tech Workforce

For the Indian diaspora and the broader technology workforce, IBM's struggles carry direct implications. The company employs close to 300,000 people globally, with only 20% based in the United States — a workforce 50% larger than Google parent Alphabet's. India remains one of IBM's largest employee bases, and any sustained revenue pressure could affect hiring and project allocations across its consulting and services divisions.

Indian-origin tech professionals tracking the AI infrastructure boom should note the trade-off at play: while demand for AI hardware and cloud engineering talent remains red-hot, companies tied to legacy enterprise systems face near-term budget pressures that may slow expansion plans.

What to Watch

The key metric in the coming quarters will be the conversion rate on deferred deals. Krishna has staked his credibility on the claim that delayed demand will materialize within six months. If significantly more than one-third of Q2's slipped deals close by year-end, it validates his thesis. If they stall, IBM's revenue forecast could face further cuts — and the stock's recovery will remain elusive. Investors will also watch whether other legacy tech giants report similar budget displacement, which would signal a sector-wide reckoning rather than an IBM-specific stumble.
